turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, it's nice to meet you too. Well, I guess what brings me in is this constant restless feeling I’ve been having. It’s like I’m wound just way too tight and I can’t fully settle down, even when I’m supposed to be doing something really calm. Like sitting through a planning meeting for work—I'm a retail buyer, so we have these endless seasonal planning meetings—or even when I'm just painting at home. 

Or yoga! I actually started taking this yoga class on Tuesday nights at that new studio downtown, the one next to the really good Italian bakery? They have the absolute best cannolis there, by the way. I usually grab one after class, which probably completely defeats the purpose of the yoga, but anyway, the instructor plays this really specific flute music that reminds me of a vendor trip I took to New Mexico a few years ago. Beautiful pottery out there, just stunning colors. But yeah, even during the quiet parts of class when everyone else is perfectly still on their mats, I just... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the restlessness. I just can't seem to sit calmly through any of it.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by unrelated thoughts about a bakery, cannolis, and a trip to New Mexico, causing them to lose their train of thought.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly reports a 'constant restless feeling,' feeling 'wound way too tight,' and an inability to settle down.
symptom_reasoning.S013: The patient describes an inability to sit calmly or settle down during quiet leisure activities like painting at home or doing yoga.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energetic or wired for several days in a row?
turns.patient_response:
Not really for several days in a row, no. I'm just kind of always at this baseline level of fidgety, I guess. Well, unless I drink way too much espresso. My husband actually bought me one of those incredibly fancy espresso machines for my 50th birthday last year. You know, the ones with the built-in bean grinder and the milk frother? It's gorgeous, all stainless steel, but it takes up half the kitchen counter, honestly. We had to completely relocate the toaster oven just to fit it, and I use that toaster oven all the time for these little flatbread pizzas I like to make on Friday nights. Friday is usually our easy dinner night. We watched this really fascinating documentary last week while we were eating, all about the history of department stores—which is obviously right up my alley with the retail buying, seeing how they used to merchandise everything in the 1920s—and... wait, I'm sorry, what was the question? 

Oh! Right, being wired for days. No, nothing like that. Just my everyday normal amount of not being able to sit still.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly states they are always at a 'baseline level of fidgety.'
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes having an 'everyday normal amount of not being able to sit still,' indicating chronic restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a long, rambling, off-topic response, demonstrating excessive talking.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly denies having periods of feeling unusually energetic or wired for several days in a row.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have this same kind of trouble sitting still and staying focused when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, actually, I really did. I remember back in elementary school, my teachers were always sending notes home to my parents because I just could not stay in my seat. I was always popping up to go look at something or talk to someone. And I was terrible about talking over my classmates, or blurting out the answer before the teacher even finished asking the question. 

I was just always in a rush, you know? Like I had to get the words out right that second. My third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—oh my gosh, she wore these incredibly bright floral dresses every single day. Like, large-scale Hawaiian prints, but we lived in Ohio, so it was a very specific look, especially in the dead of winter. She actually gave me this little squishy ball to hold under my desk to try and keep my hands busy, which was nice of her, I guess. But then one day it rolled away and went all the way to the back of the room where the reading nook was. We had this amazing beanbag chair back there, bright orange corduroy. I loved that chair. I used to try to read Nancy Drew mysteries in it, but I usually just ended up staring at the dust motes in the sunlight... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being a kid. Yeah, I've pretty much always been like this.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain focus on reading, instead ending up staring at dust motes.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility in real-time by going on a tangent and losing their train of thought, and recalls being distracted by dust motes as a child.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient notes that their teacher gave them a squishy ball specifically to keep their hands busy, indicating fidgeting.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they could not stay in their seat and were always popping up during class.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient recalls blurting out answers before the teacher had even finished asking the question.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions that they frequently talked over their classmates, indicating interrupting behavior.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself worrying a lot about many different things?
turns.patient_response:
Not really. I mean, I don't think I worry any more than the average person does. I definitely don't have that kind of constant anxiety or anything. I just get frustrated because I feel so restless. 

But worrying? No. I mean, sure, I worry about normal things, like whether a big shipment is going to clear customs in time for the spring floor set. We had this huge issue last year with a container of patio cushions that got stuck at the port in Long Beach for like three weeks. It was a total nightmare because the colors were specifically matched to this line of ceramic planters we'd already put out, and the planters were selling out fast. They were these gorgeous glazed pots, kind of a seafoam green with a crackle finish? Really heavy, though. The shipping costs on those alone were astronomical. I actually went to the factory in Vietnam where they make them, and it was fascinating to see the kilns. They had these huge wood-fired kilns, and the heat coming off them was just intense. We ate the most incredible pho from a street vendor right outside the factory gates... wait, sorry. What did you ask me? 

Oh, worrying. Right. No, I don't really sit around worrying about a bunch of different things. I'm usually moving too fast to stop and worry, to be honest.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes themselves as 'usually moving too fast to stop and worry.'
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient goes on a long, excessive tangent about patio cushions, planters, and a trip to Vietnam.
